questions.solution_text:
$x + 3 \ge 0 \implies x \ge -3$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 3, & \text{for } x \ge -3 \\ -(x + 3), & \text{for } x < -3 \end{cases}$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 3, & \text{for } x \ge -3 \\ -x - 3, & \text{for } x < -3 \end{cases}$

questions.question_text: Which piecewise definition correctly represents $f(x) = |4 - x|$?

options.why: Negated only the constant in $-(4 - x)$, writing $-4 - x$ instead of $-4 + x$.
Did not reverse the inequality when dividing by $-1$ in $4 - x \ge 0$, so the branches were attached to the wrong domains.
Made both slips: kept the inequality direction when solving $4 - x \ge 0$, and negated only the constant in $-(4 - x)$.

questions.solution_text:
$4 - x \ge 0 \implies x \le 4$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} 4 - x, & \text{for } x \le 4 \\ -(4 - x), & \text{for } x > 4 \end{cases}$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} 4 - x, & \text{for } x \le 4 \\ x - 4, & \text{for } x > 4 \end{cases}$

questions.question_text: What is the piecewise form of $f(x) = x + |x|$?

options.why: Did not negate $x$ in the negative branch where $|x| = -x$.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{For } x \ge 0: f(x) = x + x = 2x$
$\text{For } x < 0: f(x) = x + (-x) = 0$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x, & \text{for } x \ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{for } x < 0 \end{cases}$

questions.solution_text:
$x - 4 \ge 0 \implies x \ge 4$
$\text{For } x \ge 4: f(x) = (x - 4) - 2x = -x - 4$
$\text{For } x < 4: f(x) = -(x - 4) - 2x = -x + 4 - 2x = -3x + 4$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} -x - 4, & \text{for } x \ge 4 \\ -3x + 4, & \text{for } x < 4 \end{cases}$

options.why: Included the excluded point $x = 2$ in the domain.
Factored $x^2 - 4$ incorrectly or cancelled the wrong factor.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Note } x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) \text{ and } x \neq 2.$
$\text{For } x > 2: |x - 2| = x - 2 \implies f(x) = \frac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{x - 2} = x + 2$
$\text{For } x < 2: |x - 2| = -(x - 2) \implies f(x) = \frac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{-(x - 2)} = -(x + 2) = -x - 2$
$f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 2, & \text{for } x > 2 \\ -x - 2, & \text{for } x < 2 \end{cases}$
